title: Biomes
standard_text: Biomes as large regions with similar temperature and precipitation; terrestrial and aquatic biomes; and the plants and animals adapted to them. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 4, Biology)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 science worksheets (BC): what a biome is, deserts, tundra, boreal forest, temperate rainforest, grasslands and aquatic biomes, and adaptations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A biome is a large region with a similar climate.
key_sub: Temperature and precipitation decide the biome.
body_html:
How to think about it

A biome is a large region of Earth with a similar climate and similar plants and animals. Temperature and precipitation decide which biome a place is. Terrestrial biomes include desert, grassland, tundra, boreal forest and rainforest; aquatic biomes include oceans, lakes, rivers and wetlands.

BC has many biomes: temperate rainforest on the coast, dry grassland in the southern interior, boreal forest in the north and alpine tundra on high mountains. Living things have adaptations that suit their biome.

Example

A place is cold all year with no trees and frozen ground. Which biome?

Think of the far north.

Answer: tundra

Example

Why do cacti have thick stems?

Deserts are dry.

Answer: to store water

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a biome is one small habitat.
  • Thinking only hot places can be deserts (dryness matters).
  • Forgetting aquatic biomes.

faq.q: Can the same biome be on different continents?
faq.a: Yes: places with a similar climate have similar biomes, such as grasslands in Canada and Argentina.

items.q: Why can a cactus survive well in the desert?
c: It eats grass and runs fast in open land.
It has thick blubber for icy water.
It stores water in its thick stem.
It stores fat in its hump and can go a long time without water.
items.e: This trait fits the desert habitat.

items.q: Which biome has hot, wet weather all year and the most kinds of living things?
items.e: Tropical rainforests are near the equator.

items.q: What do all habitats provide for the living things there?
c: what they need to survive, like food, water and shelter
items.e: Living things need food, water, air and shelter.

items.q: Why can a frog survive well in the pond?
c: It grows well in shady, damp places.
It can live in water and on land.
It eats grass and grows a thick winter coat.
It has leaves that float on water.
items.e: This trait fits the pond habitat.

items.q: Benjamin visits the rain forest. Which living thing could NOT survive well there?
items.e: Its traits fit a different habitat.

items.q: Which biome has long, very cold winters, permafrost and no trees?
items.e: Tundra is found in the far north and on high mountains.

items.q: Why do many desert animals come out at night?
c: there is more rain at night
the Sun is brighter at night
items.e: Being nocturnal helps them save water and stay cool.

items.q: What two things mostly decide which biome a place is?
c: the number of people and cars
items.e: Biomes are grouped by similar temperature and precipitation.

items.q: In which habitat would a sea turtle survive best?
items.e: A sea turtle lives in the ocean, where it can get what it needs.

items.q: Which is an aquatic biome?
items.e: Aquatic biomes include oceans, lakes, rivers and wetlands.

items.q: In which habitat would a camel survive best?
items.e: A camel lives in the desert, where it can get what it needs.

items.q: Which habitat is very dry with little rain?
items.e: Desert plants and animals save water.

items.q: Ava visits the Arctic. Which living thing could NOT survive well there?
items.e: Its traits fit a different habitat.

items.q: What is a habitat?
c: only the food an animal eats
the place where a living thing gets the food, water, shelter and space it needs
items.e: Deserts, oceans and forests are habitats.

items.q: Which animal is best suited to the tundra?
c: a caribou with thick fur and wide hooves
items.e: Thick fur keeps it warm and wide hooves spread its weight on snow.

items.q: Why can a camel survive well in the desert?
c: It stores fat in its hump and can go a long time without water.
It has leaves that float on water.
It grows well in shady, damp places.
It hangs from branches with long claws.
items.e: This trait fits the desert habitat.

items.q: Why can a toucan survive well in the rain forest?
c: It has a long beak to reach fruit in tall trees.
It hangs from branches with long claws.
It eats grass and grows a thick winter coat.
items.e: This trait fits the rain forest habitat.

items.q: Noah visits the desert. Which living thing could NOT survive well there?
items.e: Its traits fit a different habitat.

items.q: Which biome has very little rain and plants such as cacti?
items.e: Deserts get less than about 25 cm of rain a year.

items.q: Which biome covers much of northern Canada with spruce, pine and fir trees?
items.e: The boreal forest is Canada's largest biome.

items.q: Which feature helps a pitcher plant to get nutrients that are lacking in the soil?
c: leaves shaped like jugs that trap insects
breathing roots that stick up out of the mud
large, flat leaves that float on the water
items.e: The pitcher plant has leaves shaped like jugs that trap insects.

items.q: Which adaptation helps a cactus live in a desert?
c: a thick stem that stores water
shallow roots only in wet soil
items.e: Spines instead of leaves also lose less water.

items.q: Which describes a wetland?
c: land that is soaked with water, like a marsh or bog
a frozen plain with no plants
items.e: Wetlands are aquatic biomes that clean water and are home to many birds.

items.q: Which biome would a salmon live in for most of its adult life?
items.e: Salmon hatch in fresh water, grow in the ocean and return to rivers to spawn.

items.q: Why do porcupines have quills?
items.e: Quills are a structural adaptation.

items.q: What is an adaptation?
c: a feature or behaviour that helps a living thing survive in its habitat
items.e: Adaptations can be body parts or behaviours.

items.q: A biome gets 300 cm of rain a year and stays mild. Which biome is it most likely to be?
items.e: Lots of rain supports tall, thick forests.

items.q: A duck has webbed feet. How does this help it survive?
c: It helps it get sunlight at the surface of the pond.
It helps it breathe when it is out of the water.
It helps it warm up its body.
It helps it swim in water.
items.e: This adaptation helps the duck swim in water.

items.q: Which feature helps a water lily to get sunlight at the surface of the pond?
c: breathing roots that stick up out of the mud
large, flat leaves that float on the water
eyes on the top of its head
items.e: The water lily has large, flat leaves that float on the water.

items.q: Which biome is the Okanagan Valley's dry, grassy hillside with sagebrush most like?
items.e: Parts of BC's southern interior are dry grassland.

items.q: A mudskipper has eyes on the top of its head. How does this help it survive?
c: It helps it hide from predators.
It helps it catch insects for food.
It helps it float near the surface where there is more light.
It helps it spot predators while it lies in the water.
items.e: This adaptation helps the mudskipper spot predators while it lies in the water.

items.q: Which biome has the thickest layer of frozen ground (permafrost)?
items.e: Only the top layer of tundra soil thaws in summer.

items.q: Building a highway through a forest splits a habitat in two. What is one effect?
c: Animals cannot move safely to find food or mates.
items.e: Habitat loss and fragmentation harm wildlife.

items.q: A spinifex plant has spiky, rolled-up leaves. How does this feature help it survive?
c: to lose less water and avoid the hot midday sun
to lose less water in the hot desert
to reflect sunlight and lose less water
items.e: This is a structural adaptation: a body part that helps the spinifex plant survive.

items.q: Which feature helps a mudskipper to breathe when it is out of the water?
c: large, flat leaves that float on the water
items.e: The mudskipper has gill chambers that hold water.

items.q: What is a biome?
c: a large region with a similar climate, plants and animals
items.e: Places far apart can be the same biome if their climate is similar.

items.q: Why does a snowshoe hare's fur turn white in winter?
c: to blend in with the snow and hide from predators
items.e: Camouflage helps it survive.

items.q: Why do grassland plants have deep roots?
c: to reach water in dry times and survive fires
items.e: Deep roots let grasses grow back after fire or drought.

items.q: Why do trees in the boreal forest often have needles?
c: needles lose less water and shed snow
items.e: Conifers keep their needles through the cold winter.

items.q: How did Indigenous Peoples traditionally care for the land when hunting and harvesting?
c: by taking only what they needed so plants and animals could renew
items.e: Respect for the land helps habitats stay healthy.

items.q: What do groundhogs do in winter?
c: hibernate (sleep deeply with a slow heartbeat)
items.e: Hibernation saves energy when food is scarce.

items.q: Which feature helps an eagle to catch and tear its prey?
c: sharp talons and a hooked beak
breathing roots that stick up out of the mud
leaves shaped like jugs that trap insects
items.e: The eagle has sharp talons and a hooked beak.

items.q: A small fish swims in large groups called schools. How does this help it survive?
c: It helps it stay safe, because predators find it hard to pick out one fish.
It helps it take in oxygen dissolved in the water.
It helps it lose less water.
It helps it hide from predators.
items.e: This adaptation helps the small fish stay safe, because predators find it hard to pick out one fish.

items.q: Which feature helps a frog to catch insects?
c: eyes on the top of its head
prop roots that spread out above the mud
items.e: The frog has a long, sticky tongue.

items.q: Which feature helps a fish to take in oxygen dissolved in the water?
c: a body that looks like a twig
items.e: The fish has gills.

items.q: Which action helps protect a wetland habitat?
c: keeping garbage and pollution out of it
items.e: Clean water helps the community.

items.q: Which living thing has a large throat pouch to scoop up fish from the water?
items.e: Each living thing's features fit its own habitat.

items.q: Which structural feature helps a water lily survive in its habitat?
c: thick, waxy leaves that hang down
long back legs and a long tail
items.e: The water lily has large, flat floating leaves to catch sunlight on the surface of the pond.

items.q: Which feature helps a Hydrilla plant to float near the surface where there is more light?
c: breathing roots that stick up out of the mud
items.e: The Hydrilla plant has air spaces in its stems.

items.q: Why are wildlife crossings built over some highways?
c: so animals can cross safely between parts of their habitat
to give birds a place to nest on cars
items.e: Crossings reduce road deaths.

items.q: Which feature helps a mudskipper to spot predators while it lies in the water?
c: prop roots that spread out above the mud
eyes on the top of its head
items.e: The mudskipper has eyes on the top of its head.

items.q: Which feature helps a duck to swim in water?
c: breathing roots that stick up out of the mud
items.e: The duck has webbed feet.

items.q: Which structural feature helps a spinifex plant survive in its habitat?
items.e: The spinifex plant has spiky, rolled-up leaves to lose less water in the hot desert.

items.q: A pitcher plant has leaves shaped like jugs that trap insects. How does this help it survive?
c: It helps it take in air from above the waterlogged mud.
It helps it warm up its body.
It helps it get nutrients that are lacking in the soil.
It helps it get sunlight at the surface of the pond.
items.e: This adaptation helps the pitcher plant get nutrients that are lacking in the soil.

items.q: Why do moose have long legs?
c: to walk through deep snow and marshes
items.e: Long legs suit their habitat.

items.q: Why does a beaver have a flat tail?
c: to steer in water and slap a warning
items.e: The tail is a structural adaptation.

items.q: Which feature helps a stick insect to hide from predators?
c: a body that looks like a twig
items.e: The stick insect has a body that looks like a twig.

items.q: Which structural feature helps a spinifex hopping mouse survive in its habitat?
c: long back legs and a long tail
items.e: The spinifex hopping mouse has long back legs and a long tail to leap away from predators in the sand dunes.

items.q: Which feature helps a cactus to lose less water?
items.e: The cactus has spines instead of leaves.

items.q: Which feature helps a tortoise to protect its soft body from predators?
c: a body that looks like a twig
items.e: The tortoise has a hard shell.

items.q: A factory pours waste into a river. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: Leaves fall from trees in fall. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: A new housing estate is built on a field. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: Which change could cause this: Frogs and newts lose their habitat.
c: A road is built through a wood.
Bird boxes are put up in a wood.
A pond is filled in to build a parking lot.
A nature reserve is created on old farmland.
items.e: Match the cause to the effect.

items.q: A storm blows down old trees. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: Can environments change naturally?
c: Yes, for example through seasons, floods and storms.
items.e: Natural changes happen all the time.

items.q: Why can changes to environments be dangerous to living things?
c: Living things may lose food, water or shelter.
items.e: Habitats meet needs.

items.q: Plastic litter is left on a beach. Is this change good for wildlife or harmful to wildlife?
c: it has no effect at all
items.e: People can harm habitats, but they can also protect and improve them.

items.q: A pond is filled in to build a parking lot. Is this change good for wildlife or harmful to wildlife?
c: it has no effect at all
items.e: People can harm habitats, but they can also protect and improve them.

items.q: Trees in a rainforest are cut down. What is the most likely effect on living things?
c: Animals such as orangutans lose their homes and food.
Seabirds and turtles can swallow it or get tangled.
Frogs and newts lose their habitat.
Birds and small mammals get shelter and food.
items.e: Changes to a habitat change what can live there.

items.q: Fertilizer runs off fields into a lake. Is this change good for wildlife or harmful to wildlife?
c: it has no effect at all
items.e: People can harm habitats, but they can also protect and improve them.

items.q: Lightning starts a heath fire. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: Volunteers plant trees on bare land. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: A pond is filled in to build a parking lot. What is the most likely effect on living things?
c: Animals such as orangutans lose their homes and food.
Seabirds' feathers get coated and they cannot fly or keep warm.
More birds have safe places to nest.
Frogs and newts lose their habitat.
items.e: Changes to a habitat change what can live there.

items.q: Why should we not drop litter?
c: It can harm or trap animals and spoil habitats.
items.e: Litter is dangerous.

items.q: A nature reserve is created on old farmland. Is this change good for wildlife or harmful to wildlife?
c: it has no effect at all
items.e: People can harm habitats, but they can also protect and improve them.

items.q: Bird boxes are put up in a wood. What is the most likely effect on living things?
c: Seabirds and turtles can swallow it or get tangled.
Algae grow fast and fish can die from lack of oxygen.
More birds have safe places to nest.
Seabirds' feathers get coated and they cannot fly or keep warm.
items.e: Changes to a habitat change what can live there.

items.q: A hedgerow is pulled up to make a bigger field. Is this a natural change or a change caused by people?
c: a change caused by the Moon
items.e: Some changes happen naturally; others are caused by human activity.

items.q: What is a nature reserve?
c: a protected area where wildlife is looked after
items.e: Protects habitats.

items.q: Which change could cause this: Birds and small mammals get shelter and food.
c: Trees in a rainforest are cut down.
A hedgerow is planted along a field.
Plastic litter is left on a beach.
items.e: Match the cause to the effect.

items.q: What is symbiosis?
c: a close relationship between two different species
items.e: It can be mutualism, commensalism or parasitism.

items.q: What is carrying capacity?
c: the weight an animal can carry
the number of ecosystems on Earth
the largest population an ecosystem can support
items.e: Food, water and space limit populations.

items.q: Pitcher plants catch insects because the soil is poor in nitrogen. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Few plants grow on the dark floor of a dense rainforest. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Benjamin observes that lice live on a person's head. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: What is succession?
c: the gradual change in the species in an ecosystem over time
the life cycle of a frog
items.e: A field can slowly become a forest.

items.q: Ethan needs an example of mutualism (both benefit). Which is the best example?
c: two kinds of birds eat the same insects
a tapeworm lives in an animal's intestine
oxpecker birds eat ticks off zebras
items.e: That is mutualism.

items.q: Which is an abiotic factor?
items.e: Abiotic means non-living.

items.q: A fern dries up when moved to a sunny, dry spot. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Emma observes that a bird builds a nest in a tree. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Priya needs an example of commensalism (one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed). Which is the best example?
c: trees grow taller to reach the same sunlight
fungi on plant roots get sugar and help roots take in water
a hermit crab lives in an empty snail shell
a tick sucks blood from a dog
items.e: That is commensalism.

items.q: Aiden observes that a tapeworm lives in an animal's intestine. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Nathan observes that squirrels and jays gather the same acorns. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In competition, organisms need the same limited resource.

items.q: Which organisms recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil?
items.e: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers.

items.q: Ava observes that barnacles ride on a whale without hurting it. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Maya observes that mistletoe takes water and nutrients from a tree. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Corals die when sea water becomes too warm. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: Plants grow poorly in soil that lacks nitrates. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: What is the role of producers in an ecosystem?
c: They capture the Sun's energy and make food by photosynthesis.
items.e: Producers are at the base.

items.q: Cacti survive in deserts where it rarely rains. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.
